lead: Today the Book of Genesis ends, and the Gospel of the week keeps its theme: do not be afraid. After Jacob’s death the brothers fear that Joseph will take his revenge, and Joseph answers, “Do not be afraid! Am I in the place of God? You intended to do harm to me, but God intended it for good.” In the Gospel Jesus tells the Twelve three times not to fear: not the opposition, not those who kill the body, for the Father counts every sparrow and every hair of your head. Psalm 105 calls the people to seek the Lord and his strength, and to remember the wonderful works he has done. Where it is kept, the Saturday memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary may be celebrated; the readings are those of the weekday.

set: Genesis 49 gives the last words of Jacob, who blesses each of his twelve sons. Today’s reading begins with his final charge: to be buried with his fathers in the cave at Machpelah. Chapter 50 tells of the great funeral in Canaan (50:1–14). When the brothers return to Egypt, the fear they had put aside comes back.

Background. Joseph had forgiven his brothers seventeen years earlier (45:5; 47:28). But the brothers cannot believe forgiveness is real once their protector is gone. The reading ends the book with the death of Joseph in Egypt, in a coffin, and with a promise: God will come and lead the people up to the land he swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Genesis ends in a coffin and in hope. The Lectionary leaves out 49:33 and 50:1–14, the death and burial of Jacob.
str: 49:29–32: Jacob’s charge: bury me with my ancestors at Machpelah, the field Abraham bought.
50:15–18: the brothers fear that Joseph will repay them; they send a message in Jacob’s name and fall down before him.
50:19–21: Joseph weeps, says “Do not be afraid! Am I in the place of God?” and promises to provide for them.
50:22–26: Joseph lives one hundred ten years; he foretells that God will come, makes the Israelites swear to carry up his bones, and dies.
kw: The same verb is used twice in v. 20: you “intended” evil, God “intended” it for good. The same event has two authors: human sin and divine providence, and God’s purpose wins.
“God will surely come to you” (v. 24). The verb is used again in Exodus 3:16, when God visits his people in their slavery. It means a coming with power to save.
The Hebrew of v. 21 says Joseph “spoke to their hearts”. It is the language of tenderness (Hosea 2:14). Forgiveness here is not only a verdict but a tender word.
vv: There Abraham and his wife Sarah were buried; there Isaac and his wife Rebekah were buried; and there I buried Leah
Jacob lists the graves of his family. The only piece of the promised land the patriarchs own is a tomb, and Jacob wants to lie there in hope that the land will one day be his people’s.
What if Joseph still bears a grudge against us
Guilt does not believe in forgiveness easily. The brothers judge Joseph by their own hearts.
Do not be afraid! Am I in the place of God?
Joseph refuses to take the place of the judge. Vengeance belongs to God alone (Deuteronomy 32:35).
Even though you intended to do harm to me, God intended it for good, in order to preserve a numerous people, as he is doing today.
The summit of the Joseph story. It does not say that the wrong was right. It says that God is greater than evil and can bring good out of it.
In this way he reassured them, speaking kindly to them.
Forgiveness is shown by both providing and speaking tenderly. Joseph promises food and he comforts.
you shall carry up my bones from here.

Joseph’s hope looks beyond Egypt. His bones were carried out at the Exodus (Exodus 13:19) and buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32). The Letter to the Hebrews names this as an act of faith (Hebrews 11:22).
ch: The Catechism uses the words of Joseph to teach that God can bring good out of evil: it is one of the great examples in Scripture (CCC 312, quoting Genesis 50:20). The Church also reads the end of Genesis as a sign of hope against the grave. Joseph, who forgave and fed those who had harmed him, has long been seen as a figure of Christ, who prayed for those who crucified him and who gives himself as bread. Christians, as the Catechism says of forgiveness, ask for the grace to do what Joseph did (CCC 2843). The reading is also, first of all, the Jewish people’s own story of the end of the patriarchs and the beginning of the people of Israel.

r.h: You are of more value than many sparrows
set: The mission discourse of chapter 10 now comes to its centre: three times in vv. 26, 28 and 31 Jesus says “do not fear”. The disciples will be maligned as their master was. Matthew places this teaching just after the warning of persecution, to show that fear is answered by trust in the Father.

Background. In Jewish households a slave or pupil was bound to his master or teacher. “Beelzebul” in v. 25 is the name the opponents gave to the prince of demons when they accused Jesus (12:24; compare 9:34). To call the master of the house this is to call his whole household the same. A sparrow was the cheapest food in the market, sold for a small coin; in Luke the price is five sparrows for two coins (Luke 12:6).
str: vv. 24–25: the disciple is like the teacher; if they malign the master, they will malign his household.
vv. 26–27: do not fear: what is hidden will be revealed; proclaim from the housetops what you hear in secret.
vv. 28–31: do not fear those who kill the body; the Father knows each sparrow and counts each hair; you are of more value.
vv. 32–33: whoever acknowledges Jesus before others, Jesus acknowledges before the Father; whoever denies him, he denies.
kw: Perhaps “Baal the prince”, from the name of a pagan god (the origin of the name is debated); the Gospels use it for the prince of demons (12:24). The opponents of Jesus used it to belittle his power over evil spirits.

The verb appears with and without “not” in vv. 26–31. The Bible distinguishes the fear that paralyses from the reverent fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7) and delivers us from every other fear.
Literally “to say the same thing”: to speak out for Jesus, as he speaks for us. The word later becomes the word for a confession of faith.
vv: A disciple is not above the teacher, nor a slave above the master;
Discipleship means sharing the master’s way, including its cost. The disciple is not exempt from what the Master meets.
What I say to you in the dark, tell in the light; and what you hear whispered, proclaim from the housetops.
Jesus taught his disciples in private, but the teaching is for all. The flat roofs of Palestine were a natural place for a public announcement.
Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell.

Most Fathers and commentators understand “him who can destroy” as God, the true judge (compare Luke 12:5). The sense is that nothing human is to frighten the disciple more than the loss of fellowship with God.
Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father.
God’s care reaches the smallest of creatures. Not “without his knowledge” only, but within the knowledge and love of the Father.
And even the hairs of your head are all counted.
A picture of the attention of a father’s love. There is nothing about you that is overlooked.
So do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.
The argument from lesser to greater: if the Father cares for sparrows, how much more for his children.
ch: The Catechism quotes vv. 29–31 when it teaches about divine providence: Jesus asks for a childlike abandonment to the care of our heavenly Father, who looks after the smallest needs of his children (CCC 305). Verses 32–33 are the root of the Christian duty to confess the faith openly; the Catechism teaches that the Christian must not be ashamed to bear witness to the Lord (CCC 2471). The Church also teaches that the one who confesses Christ before others is acknowledged by Christ before the Father, and the one who denies him is denied; this is a call to fidelity and not a threat to the weak, for Peter who denied was forgiven (John 21:15–17).

qa: Does Jesus tell us to fear God, or not to fear?

Both, but in two different senses. We are never to fear in the sense of terror at a God who wants our harm: “do not be afraid” runs through the whole passage, and the Father numbers the hairs of our head. But the Bible keeps a holy fear of God, a reverent awe and a horror of losing him through sin, which is the beginning of wisdom. The Catechism teaches that the fear of the Lord is a gift of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1831).
study: The brothers could not quite believe in Joseph’s forgiveness. Where do I find it hard to believe that God has really forgiven me?
Which of my fears is the Father’s word “you are of more value than many sparrows” speaking to today?
